Stephen accused Formosus of perjury and of having acceded to the papacy illegally.  At the end of the trial, Formosus was pronounced guilty and his papacy retroactively declared null.
Pope John V | Pope John V (Latin: "Ioannes V" ; d. August 2, 686) was Pope from consecration 23 July 685 to his death in 686.  He was the first pope of the Byzantine Papacy allowed to be consecrated by the Byzantine Emperor without prior consent, and the first in a line of ten consecutive popes of Eastern origin.  His papacy was marked by reconciliation between the city of Rome and the Empire.

He was said to have been Pope after another Pope John who reigned four months after Pope John XIV (983–984) and was named "Papa Ioannes XIV Bis" or "Pope John XIVb".  This supposed second John XIV never existed, rather he was confused with a certain cardinal deacon John, son of Robert, who was opposed to Boniface VII and is now excluded from the papal lists.
Pope John VII | Pope John VII (Latin: "Ioannes VII" ; c. 650 – 18 October 707) was Pope from 1 March 705 to his death in 707.  The successor of John VI, he was (like his predecessor) of Greek ancestry.  He is one of the popes of the Byzantine Papacy.

Papal conclave, 1903 | The Papal conclave of 1903 followed the death of the 93-year-old Pope Leo XIII, who at his death was the second-longest reigning "elected" pope in history.  (Pope John Paul II (r. 1978–2005) passed Leo a century later.)
Papal conclave, 1521–22 | The papal conclave, 1521–1522 elected Pope Adrian VI to succeed Pope Leo X.  The conclave was marked by the early candidacies of cardinal-nephew Giulio de'Medici (future Pope Clement VII) and Alessandro Farnese (future Pope Paul III), although the Colonna and other cardinals blocked their election.
